Suppose $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a sequence of random variables representing a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a population with the population mean $\mu.$ 
Then, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is given by

$$
\overline{X} 
= \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$

Note that:

- $\overline{X}$ is the mean value of $X_1,X_2,\ldots, X_n,$ while $\bar{x}$ is the mean of a specific sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n,$

- the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is an estimator of the population mean $\mu,$ and

- the value $\hat{\mu} = \bar{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean $\mu.$

Therefore, our estimate for the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\mu } & =\overset{―}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{7}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{7}(6+13+7+5+14+11+7) \\  & =\frac{63}{7} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables $X_i$ as follows:
![](images/41/412ed703d6c44b1e664317fd734871cfe71d14c944cfa9f9bca84752f635836e.svg)

Now, provided that $N \gg n,$ we have that

$$
X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \approx B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\widehat{\,p}  = \overline{X} = \dfrac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p} ] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p} ] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p = 42 \% = 0.42,$ and $n = 40.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =42%=0.42, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.42(1-0.42)}{40} \\  & ≈0.0061\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

Suppose we have a set of observed frequencies $O_i$ and corresponding expected frequencies $E_i$, as defined by a theoretical model under the null hypothesis. Then, the random variable

$$
X = \sum_{i} \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}
$$

approximately follows a chi-square distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom, where

- $O_i$ is the observed frequency for category $i$, and
- $E_i$ is the expected frequency for category $i$, as predicted under the null hypothesis.

This approximation holds when all expected frequencies $E_i$ are sufficiently large (typically

$$
E_i \geq 5
$$

for each category), and the observations are independent.

Let $Y$ be the number of customer complaints received per week. Under the null hypothesis, we have that $Y \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$.

The number of observations is

$$
N = 20+12+8 =40
$$

We can calculate an estimator for $\lambda$, which we denote as $\hat \lambda$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ^(^) &= \frac{total number of events}{total number of observations} \\
&= (∑(y_{i} \cdot O_{i}))/(N)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $O_i$ is the observed frequency for the $i$th observation, $N$ is the number of observations. So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ^(^) &= \frac{0 \cdot 20 + 1 \cdot 12 + 2 \cdot 8}{40} \\
&= 0.7
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the proposed distribution is $Y\sim \mathrm{Po}(0.7)$.

Under the hypothesis that $Y \sim \mathrm{Po}(0.7)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(Y = y) &= \frac{λ^{y}e^{- λ}}{y!} \\
&= ((0.7)^{y}e^{-0.7})/(y!), y = 0, 1, 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Let's calculate the probability of each value of $Y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(Y = 0) &= ((0.7)^{0}e^{-0.7})/(0!) \approx 0.496585 \\
P(Y = 1) &= ((0.7)^{1}e^{-0.7})/(1!) \approx 0.347610 \\
P(Y = 2) &= ((0.7)^{2}e^{-0.7})/(2!) \approx 0.121663 \\
P(Y \ge 3) &= 1 - P(Y = 0) - P(Y = 1) - P(Y = 2) = 0.034142
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the expected frequencies for each observation are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{0} &= N \cdot P(Y = 0) = 40 \cdot 0.496585 \approx 19.8634 \\
E_{1} &= N \cdot P(Y = 1) = 40 \cdot 0.347610 \approx 13.9044 \\
E_{2} &= N \cdot P(Y = 2) = 40 \cdot 0.121663 \approx 4.8665 \\
E_{3} &= N \cdot P(Y \ge 3) = 40 \cdot 0.034142 \approx 1.3657
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that there are two frequencies less than $5$, so we combine the values $Y = 2$ and $Y=3$.

A table summarizing the observed and corresponding theoretical frequencies is given below:

| $y_i$ | $0$ | $1$ | $\geq2$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $O_i$ | $20$ | $12$ | $8$ |
| $E_i$ | $19.8634$ | $13.9044$ | $6.2322$ |
| $\dfrac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i}$ | $0.0009$ | $0.2608$ | $0.5014$ |

We have rounded values to four decimal places, where appropriate.

We compute our test statistic by summing the last row:

$$
\begin{aligned}
∑_(i)((O_{i} - E_{i})^{2})/(E_{i}) &= 0.0009 + 0.2608 + 0.5014 \\
&\approx 0.8
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the test statistic is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.8}$ (rounded to one decimal place).

Our data has two constraints: the total number of observations must equal $N$, and the estimated rate $\hat \lambda$. Therefore, the number of degrees of freedom $\nu$ is calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
ν &= number of categories - number of constraints \\
&= 3 - 2 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch Out!** We must use the number of categories in the combined table!

So, there is

$$
\nu = \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}
$$

degree of freedom.

From the given chi-square table, the critical value for $\nu = 1$ at a $10\%$ significance level is

$$
\chi^2_{\textrm{critical}} = 2.706
$$

and the critical region is

$$
X\geq 2.706
$$

as shown below.

![](images/15/155070611813bc121d3af67bb5e53c5504bfa3e089a4b0b1d491e8f351f36bc7.png)

Our test statistic $(0.8)$ is not inside the critical region. Therefore, there is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{insufficient}}$ evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

| Observations $(y_i)$ | Frequency $(O_i)$ | $y_i^{\textrm{mid}}$ |

| $9\leq y_i < 13$ | $25$ | $11$ |

\end{aligned}

$$

![](images/3f/3f28000117b2d51899700d0e995c44e556f15be3d740cbac98e4e1a3c95ff709.png)

Our test statistic $(12.6)$ lies inside the critical region. Therefore, there is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{sufficient}}$ evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=45%=0.45,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =45%=0.45, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.45(1-0.45)}{20} \\  & ≈0.0124\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

Let's remind ourselves how to estimate $\mu$ and $\sigma$ from sample data.

Suppose $Y$ is a continuous random variable. A random sample is carried out, and the sample data is shown below.

| Observations $(y_i)$ | Frequency $(O_i)$ |
| --- | ---: |
| $1\leq y_i < 3$ | $8$ |
| $3\leq y_i < 5$ | $12$ |
| $5\leq y_i < 7$ | $11$ |
| $7\leq y_i < 9$ | $9$ |

Suppose we wish to test the following null and alternative hypotheses:

- $H_0:\:$ $Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$
- $H_1:\:$ $Y\not\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$

We're not given the mean $\mu$ nor the variance $\sigma^2$, so we have to estimate them from the sample data.

- For the mean, we have the following estimate:
$μ^(^)|= \frac{weighted sum of the midpoints}{total number of observations}; = \frac{1}{N}∑_(i)O_{i} \cdot y_{i}^{mid}$
- For the variance, we have
$\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \dfrac{1}{N-1}\sum_i O_i \cdot (y_i^{\textrm{mid}} - \widehat{\mu})^2$
where $\widehat{\mu}$ is our estimate for the mean $\mu$, $\widehat{\sigma}^2$ is our estimate for the variance $\sigma^2$,$N$ is the total number of observations, $y_i^{\textrm{mid}}$ is the midpoint of an observational class $(a_i, b_i)$.

Let's compute estimates for the mean and variance in this case:

The total number of observations is

$$
N= 8+12+11+9= 40
$$

Next, we find the midpoint of each observational class.

| Observations $(y_i)$ | Frequency $(O_i)$ | $y_i^{\textrm{mid}}$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $1\leq y_i < 3$ | $8$ | $2$ |
| $3\leq y_i < 5$ | $12$ | $4$ |
| $5\leq y_i < 7$ | $11$ | $6$ |
| $7\leq y_i < 9$ | $9$ | $8$ |

Our estimate $\widehat{\mu}$ for the mean $\mu$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
μ^(^) &= \frac{1}{N}∑O_{i} \cdot y_{i}^{mid} \\
&= \frac{1}{40}(8 \cdot 2 + 12 \cdot 4 + 11 \cdot 6 + 9 \cdot 8) \\
&= 5.05
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, our estimate $\widehat{\sigma}^2$ for the variance $\sigma^2$ is

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\hat{\sigma }}^{2} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{1}{N - 1}} \sum  {O}_{i} \cdot  ( {y}_{i}^{\text{mid}} - \hat{\mu } {)}^{2} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{1}{40 - 1}} ( 8 \cdot  ( 2 - 5.05 {)}^{2} + 12 \cdot  ( 4 - 5.05 {)}^{2} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  \phantom{=} \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} + 11 \cdot  ( 6 - 5.05 {)}^{2} + 9 \cdot  ( 8 - 5.05 {)}^{2} ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 4.51025 \ldots  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  \approx  \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{ {\color{blue}4.5}} .\end{array}}
$$

When conducting a chi-square test, we lose a degree of freedom for every estimated parameter:

- If *only one* parameter must be estimated, then we have two constraints in total, and
$\nu = \textrm{number of categories} - 2$.
- If *both* parameters must be estimated, then we have three constraints in total, and
$\nu = \textrm{number of categories} - 3$.

Let's see an example.

$$
S=\{0,1,2,3\}
$$

A random sample is carried out, and the sample data is shown below.

| Observation $(x_i)$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Observed Frequency $(O_i)$ | $12$ | $32$ | $44$ | $12$ |

Suppose we wish to conduct a chi-square goodness-of-fit test with the following null and alternative hypotheses:

- $H_0:\:$ The sample data fit a binomial distribution $B(3,p)$
- $H_1:\:$ The sample data does not fit a binomial distribution $B(3,p)$

Notice we're not given the success probability $p$. Therefore, we must estimate it from the sample data, which we can do as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p^(^) &= \frac{total number of successes}{total number of trials} \\
&= (∑(x_{i} \cdot O_{i}))/(n \cdot N)
\end{aligned}
$$

where

- $\hat p$ is our estimate of the success probability $p$,
- $N$ is the number of observations,
- $n$ is the number of trials in each binomial sequence.

In our case, we have the following:

- The total number of observations is given by
$N=12+32+44+ 12= 100$.
- The number of trials in each binomial sequence is
$n=3$.

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
p^(^) &= (0 \cdot 12 + 1 \cdot 32 + 2 \cdot 44 + 3 \cdot 12)/(3 \cdot (100)) \\
&= 0.52
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the proposed distribution is $B(3,0.52)$.

Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/46/4624ca7ee7660803ddc7165252c3725030b13ab255f56dc5d87e23090c2363bf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ 

We know that if the population sample size $n$ is small compared to the population size $N,$ then the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables. Therefore,

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).
$$

Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. Therefore, we can form an *estimate* for the population proportion $p$ as follows:

$$
\widehat{\,p} =  \dfrac{X}{n} = \dfrac1 n \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i =  \overline{X}
$$

Let's calculate the mean and variance of $\widehat{\,p}.$ First, recall that

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).
$$

 

Therefore, for the mean of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{E}[\frac{X}{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot \text{E}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot np \\  & =p.\end{aligned}
$$

For the variance of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{X}{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot np(1-p) \\  & =\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we have the following important results:

$$
\textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}
$$

It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is, it has mean $p$ and variance $\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.$

Finally, consider an $n$th-order linear differential equation

$$
y^{(n)} + a_{n-1}(x)y^{(n-1)} + \cdots + a_1(x)y' + a_0(x)y = g(x),
$$

and let $\{y_1,\dots,y_n\}$ be a set of fundamental solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation.

Now, we’ll derive formulas for the method of variation of parameters.

A particular solution can be written as

$$
y_p(x) = u_1(x)y_1(x) + \cdots + u_n(x)y_n(x).
$$

To find $u_1,\dots,u_n$, we impose $n-1$ auxiliary conditions:

$$
\sum_{j=1}^n u_j'(x)y_j^{(k)}(x) = 0,
\qquad
k=0,1,\dots,n-2,
$$

which leads to the final equation

$$
\sum_{j=1}^n u_j'(x)y_j^{(n-1)}(x) = g(x).
$$

Together, these $n$ equations form a linear system for $u_1'(x),\dots,u_n'(x)$ of the form

$$
Y \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{g},
$$

where

$$
(\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} & ⋯ & {y}_{n} \\ {y}_{1}^{'} & {y}_{2}^{'} & ⋯ & {y}_{n}^{'} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ {y}_{1}^{(n-2)} & {y}_{2}^{(n-2)} & ⋯ & {y}_{n}^{(n-2)} \\ {y}_{1}^{(n-1)} & {y}_{2}^{(n-1)} & ⋯ & {y}_{n}^{(n-1)}\end{aligned})
$$

Now, recall that $W(x) = \det(Y)$ is the Wronskian. And for each $i=1,\dots,n,$ define:

- $\widehat{W}_i(x)$ as the determinant obtained by replacing the $i$th column of $Y$ with $\mathbf{g},$ and

- $W_i(x)$ as the determinant obtained by deleting the $n$th (final) row and the $i$th column from $Y.$

Notice that, since $\mathbf{g}$ has zeroes in all components except for the final one (which is equal to $g(x)$), by the properties of determinants we can expand $\widehat{W}_i(x)$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\overset{^}{W}}_{i}(x) & =(-1)^{n+i}g(x){W}_{i}(x) \\  & =(-1)^{n-i}g(x){W}_{i}(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we used that $(-1)^{n+i} = (-1)^{n-i}$ because the exponents differ by an even number, $2i.$

Next, by *Cramer's rule*, we get

$$
u'_i = \dfrac{\widehat{W}_i(x)}{W(x)} = (-1)^{n-i} \frac{g(x)\,W_i(x)}{W(x)},
\qquad
i=1,\dots,n,
$$

and integrating both sides (setting the constant of integration to zero), we obtain

$$
u_i(x) = (-1)^{n-i}\int \frac{g(x)\,W_i(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x,
\qquad
i=1,\dots,n.
$$

Finally, the general solution is

$$
y(x)=u_1y_1(x)+\cdots+u_ny_n(x)+y_p(x).
$$

Given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,p} \pm \overbrace{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}}^{\large \textrm{margin of error}}
$$

where

- $\!\widehat{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,
- $p$ is the population proportion,
- $n$ is the sample size,
- $P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ and $Z \sim N(0,1)$.

If we require the margin of error to be at most $\varepsilon$, then

$$
z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}} \leq \varepsilon \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad n \geq \dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 \, \widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{\varepsilon^2}
$$

We are interested in finding a $95\%$ confidence interval. So, we have

$$
\alpha=1-0.95=0.05 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025
$$

We are given that

$$
P(Z > 1.96) = 0.025
$$

As a result,

$$
z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.025} = 1.96
$$

We're given the estimate

$$
\widehat{\,p} = 84\% = 0.84
$$

Therefore, substituting

$$
\varepsilon=0.06, \qquad \widehat{\,p}=0.84, \qquad z_{\alpha/2}=1.96
$$

into the inequality for $n$, we obtain

$$
n \mid \ge (z_{α/2}^{2}p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(ε^{2}); = ((1.96)^{2}0.84(1 - 0.84))/((0.06)^{2}); = 143.42
$$

Finally, rounding up to the nearest integer, we get that

$$
n=\bbox[3pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue}144}
$$

or larger.

$$

$$

$$

is the minimum sample size needed when the population is large.

$$

$$

Suppose we have a contingency table in which a feature with $m$ levels is examined on $n$ samples from different populations. Then, the random variable

$$
X = \sum_{i} \sum_{j} \frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}
$$

approximately follows a chi-square distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom, where

- $O_{ij}$ is the observed frequency for population $i$ and feature level $j$, and
- $E_{ij}$ is the expected frequency for population $i$ and feature level $j$, as predicted under the null hypothesis that the distribution of the feature is the same in the two populations.

Given that $N_1, N_2, \ldots, N_n$ are the sample sizes and

$$
N=N_1 + \ldots + N_n
$$

is the grand sample size, the expected frequencies can be calculated as follows:

$$
E_{ij} = N_i \cdot \widehat p_j
$$

where $\widehat p_i$ is the proportion of individuals with value $A_i$ in the grand sample.

This approximation holds when all expected frequencies $E_{ij}$ are sufficiently large (typically

$$
E_{ij} \geq 5
$$

for each cell), and the observations are independent.

In our case, we have a sample of $N_1 = 180$ voters from Region A (population 1) and a sample of $N_2 = 120$ voters from Region B (population 2).

First, we estimate the probability $\widehat{p}_{X}$ of a randomly selected voter choosing Candidate X.

$$
\begin{aligned}
p^(^)_{X} &= \frac{110 + 70}{300} = 0.6
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the probability $\widehat{p}_{Y}$ of that a randomly selected voter chooses Candidate Y is

$$
\begin{aligned}
p^(^)_{Y} &= 1 - p^(^)_{X} = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the expected frequencies for each cell under the assumption that the distribution of votes is the same across both populations can be estimated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{11} &= p^(^)_{X} \cdot N_{1} = 0.6 \cdot 180 = 108 \\
E_{12} &= p^(^)_{Y} \cdot N_{1} = 0.4 \cdot 180 = 72 \\
E_{21} &= p^(^)_{X} \cdot N_{2} = 0.6 \cdot 120 = 72 \\
E_{22} &= p^(^)_{Y} \cdot N_{2} = 0.4 \cdot 120 = 48
\end{aligned}
$$

So, our table now looks as follows:

|  | Candidate X | Candidate Y |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Region A | $O_{11}\|= 110; E_{11}\|= 108$ | $O_{12}\|= 70; E_{12}\|= 72$ |
| Region B | $O_{21}\|= 70; E_{21}\|= 72$ | $O_{22}\|= 50; E_{22}\|= 48$ |

Notice that all of the expected frequencies are greater than or equal to $5$.

Now, we calculate the term

$$
\dfrac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}
$$

for each combination of value and population:

$$
\begin{aligned}
((O_{11} - E_{11})^{2})/(E_{11}) &= ((110 - 108)^{2})/(108) \approx 0.0370 \\
((O_{12} - E_{12})^{2})/(E_{12}) &= ((70 - 72)^{2})/(72) \approx 0.0556 \\
((O_{21} - E_{21})^{2})/(E_{21}) &= ((70 - 72)^{2})/(72) \approx 0.0556 \\
((O_{22} - E_{22})^{2})/(E_{22}) &= ((50 - 48)^{2})/(48) \approx 0.0833
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we rounded to four decimal places.

First, we compute our test statistic by summing the above results:

$$
\begin{aligned}
X &= ∑_(i)∑_(j)((O_{ij} - E_{ij})^{2})/(E_{ij}) \\
&= 0.0370 + 0.0556 + 0.0556 + 0.0833 \\
&\approx 0.2
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the test statistic is approximately $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.2}$.

Next, we compute the degrees of freedom:

- Given a contingency table with $n$ populations and $m$ levels of a feature: the number of constraints is $1 + (m-1) + (n-1)$ the total number of observations must equal $N$, the estimates $\widehat p_1, \widehat p_2,\ldots \widehat p_{m-1}$ and $N_1, N_2, \ldots N_{n-1}$ set a constraint each. Notice that the $\widehat p_m$ and $N_n$ can be deduced by the others, so they don't create a constraint. Therefore, the number of degrees of freedom $\nu$ is calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
ν &= number of cells - number of constraints \\
&= nm - 1 - (n - 1) - (m - 1) \\
&= nm - n - m + 1 \\
&= (n - 1)(m - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

So, in our case there is

$$
\nu = (2-1)(2-1)=\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}
$$

degree of freedom.

From the given chi-square table, the critical value for $\nu=1$ at a $10\%$ significance level is

$$
\chi^2_{\textrm{critical}}=2.706
$$

and the critical region is

$$
X\geq 2.706
$$

as shown below.

![](images/dc/dcf4f6d388a82cbfcd89b77a0c441c2774aaee3a95a9f983fb6c484dbba37959.png)

Our test statistic $(0.2)$ lies outside the critical region. Therefore, there is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{insufficient}}$ evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

So, we conclude that there is no evidence that the vote distribution varies across different regions.

Since $n=80$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=0.75,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=80\cdot 0.7=56>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=80\cdot (1-0.7)=24>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.05}=1.645.
$$

Therefore, a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.7\pm 1.645\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.7(1-0.7)}{80}} \\  & 0.7\pm 0.084\end{aligned}
$$

We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=80.6+5x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}$ is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{{S}_{xx}}}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=80.6+5x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}=5.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $95%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

We are given that $P(T>4.303)=0.025.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.025}=4.303.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(3-6)^{2}+(5-6)^{2}+(7-6)^{2}+(9-6)^{2} \\  & =9+1+1+9 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=4.303\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.35}{20}}≈0.6
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=5\pm 0.6
$$

Given a contingency table with $n$ levels for the row factor $A_1, A_2, \ldots A_n$ and $m$ levels for the column factor $B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_m$, under the hypothesis that the factors are independent, we have that the probability of an individual having the value $A_i$ for the row factor and the value $B_j$ for the column factor is equal to the product of the probabilities:

$$
P(A_i \cap B_j) = P(A_i) \cdot P(B_j), \qquad i=1,2,\ldots, n \quad j=1,2,\ldots, m
$$

We can calculate estimates for the probabilities $P(A_i)$ and $P(B_j)$, which we denote as $\hat p(A_i)$ and $\hat p(B_j)$, respectively, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p^(^)(A_{i}) &= \frac{number of observations with levelA_{i}}{total number of observations} \\
p^(^)(B_{j}) &= \frac{number of observations with levelB_{j}}{total number of observations}
\end{aligned}
$$

For a sample of size $N$, the expected frequency $E_{ij}$ of the event $A_i\cap B_j$ under the assumption of independence is given by

$$
E_{ij} = N\cdot P(A_i\cap B_j)
$$

Let's see another example.

before:
Suppose we conduct a random sample to find the proportion of voters who intend to vote for a particular candidate in an upcoming election. Let's assume we initially used a sample of size $n_1$ to construct a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$.

After completing the initial survey, it's decided that a new sample must be carried out, and the resulting confidence interval should have the following features:

- The confidence level of the new confidence interval should be $95\%$ (unchanged).
- The new confidence interval should be one-half as wide as the original (increased precision).

To increase the precision while keeping the confidence level fixed, we'll need to *increase* the sample size. But by how much? Let's determine how much larger the second sample size $n_2$ should be compared to the first to satisfy the new conditions.

First, recall that, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,p} \pm \overbrace{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}}^{\large \textrm{margin of error}}
$$

where

- $\!\widehat{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,
- $p$ is the population proportion,
- $n$ is the sample size,
- $P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ and $Z \sim N(0,1)$.

Given a particular margin of error $\varepsilon$, we can deduce an approximate sample size:

$$
z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}} = \varepsilon \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad n = \dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 \, \widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{\varepsilon^2}
$$

Let $\varepsilon_1$ and $\varepsilon_2$ be the margins of error of the confidence intervals $I_1$ and $I_2$, respectively. Since we want $I_2$ to half the length of $I_1$, we must have

$$
\varepsilon_1 = 2\varepsilon_2
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_{1} &= (z_{α/2}^{2}p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(ε_{1}^{2}), \\
n_{2} &= (z_{α/2}^{2}p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(ε_{2}^{2}), \\
\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} &= \frac{ε_{2}^{2}}{ε_{1}^{2}} \\
&= (\frac{ε_{2}}{ε_{1}})^{2} \\
&= (\frac{1}{2})^{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
4 n_1 = n_2
$$

Suppose we conduct a random sample to find the proportion of voters who intend to vote for a particular candidate in an upcoming election. Let's assume we initially used a sample of size $n_1$ to construct a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$.

After completing the initial survey, it's decided that a new sample must be carried out, and the resulting confidence interval should have the following features:

- The confidence level of the new confidence interval should be $95\%$ (unchanged).
- The new confidence interval should be one-half as wide as the original (increased precision).

To increase the precision while keeping the confidence level fixed, we'll need to *increase* the sample size. But by how much? Let's determine how much larger the second sample size $n_2$ should be compared to the first to satisfy the new conditions.

First, recall that, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,p} \pm \overbrace{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}}^{\large \textrm{margin of error}}
$$

where

- $\!\widehat{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,
- $p$ is the population proportion,
- $n$ is the sample size,
- $P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ and $Z \sim N(0,1)$.

Given a particular margin of error $\varepsilon$, we can deduce an approximate sample size:

$$
z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}} = \varepsilon \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad n = \dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 \, \widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{\varepsilon^2}
$$

Let $\varepsilon_1$ and $\varepsilon_2$ be the margins of error of the confidence intervals $I_1$ and $I_2$, respectively. Since we want $I_2$ to half the length of $I_1$, we must have

$$
\varepsilon_1 = 2\varepsilon_2
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_{1} &= (z_{α/2}^{2}\widehat{p}(1 - \widehat{p}))/(ε_{1}^{2}), \\
n_{2} &= (z_{α/2}^{2}\widehat{p}(1 - \widehat{p}))/(ε_{2}^{2}), \\
\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} &= \frac{ε_{2}^{2}}{ε_{1}^{2}} \\
&= (\frac{ε_{2}}{ε_{1}})^{2} \\
&= (\frac{1}{2})^{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
4 n_1 = n_2
$$

Therefore, $n_2$ must be $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\text{larger}}$ then $n_1$ by a factor of approximately $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}4}$.

Suppose we wish to carry out the following hypothesis test:

- $H_0: p_1 = p_2$
- $H_1: p_1 > p_2$

As we just saw, the variance of the difference between the two sampling distributions is

$$
\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}
$$

Now, under the null hypothesis, the two proportions are equal. Thus, assuming that $H_0$ is true, we can set

$$
p_1 = p_2 = p
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var[p^(^)_{1} - p^(^)_{2}] &= (p(1 - p))/(n_{1}) + (p(1 - p))/(n_{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var[p^(^)_{1} - p^(^)_{2}] &= p(1 - p)(\frac{1}{n_{1}} + \frac{1}{n_{2}})
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the two proportions are equal under the null hypothesis, we can use a **pooled estimate** $\overline{p}$ of the shared proportion $p$ to form a point estimate.

$$
\overline{p} = \dfrac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2} = \dfrac{n_1\widehat{\,p}_1+n_2\widehat{\,p}_2}{n_1+n_2}
$$

where $x_1$ and $x_2$ give the number of sample elements from the first and second samples, respectively, with the characteristic.

Thus, our estimate for the variance is

$$
\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] =\overline{p}(1-\overline{p})\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}\right)
$$

This is similar to the pooled variance estimate we saw in a previous lesson.

As a result, we can use the following normal approximation:

$$
\dfrac {(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)} {\sqrt{\overline{p}(1-\overline{p}) \left(\dfrac{1}{n_1}+\dfrac{1}{n_2} \right)} \phantom{\mid}} \sim N(0,1)
$$

Note the following:

- A pooled variance estimate is preferable to an unpooled estimate when the null hypothesis assumes $p_1 = p_2$. It can be shown that the standard error of the pooled estimate is lower than the unpooled one, making our hypothesis test more reliable.
- On the other hand, suppose we have the following null hypothesis:
$H_0: p_1 - p_2 = k \neq 0$.
In this case, the variances cannot be assumed equal, and we must use an unpooled estimate for the variance, i.e.,
$\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}$.

In this lesson, we'll only consider null hypotheses of the form $p_1 = p_2$.

We can conduct hypothesis tests to determine whether two variables are independent. Suppose we want to determine whether the pass rates of students sitting a particular math exam are independent of the school they attend. The district superintendent conducts a random sample of $60$ students who sat the exam from two schools in the district, and they get the following two-way frequency table (also called a **contingency table**) of results. | | Pass | Fail | | --- | ---: | ---: | | School 1 | $18$ | $6$ | | School 2 | $24$ | $12$ | This is a $2\times 2$ contingency table because we have two levels for the row factors (School 1 and School 2) and two for the column factors (Pass and Fail). We wish to test the following hypotheses: - $H_0:\:\:$ The pass rates are independent of the choice of school - $H_1:\:\:$ The pass rates are *not* independent of the choice of school The first step in conducting our hypothesis test is calculating the **expected frequency** for every possible outcome, assuming that the null hypothesis is true. First, we must find the probabilities associated with each row factor, i.e., we must find $P(\textrm{Student is from School 1}), \qquad P(\textrm{Student is from School 2})$ and for each column factor $P(\textrm{Student passes}), \qquad P(\textrm{Student fails})$. We're not given these probabilities. However, they can be estimated from the sample data. We'll use the notation $\hat p(A)$ to denote our sample estimate of $P(A){:}$ So, in our case, we have: $$ \begin{aligned} p^(^)(Student is from School 1) &= \frac{18 + 6}{60} = 0.4 \\ p^(^)(Student is from School 2) &= \frac{24 + 12}{60} = 0.6 \\ p^(^)(Student passes the exam) &= \frac{18 + 24}{60} = 0.7 \\ p^(^)(Student fails the exam) &= \frac{6 + 12}{60} = 0.3 \end{aligned} $$ Recall that if two events $A$ and $B$ are independent, then $$ P(A\cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B) $$ Let's estimate the probability of each combination of values of $A$ and $B$ *under the assumption of independence:* $$ \begin{aligned} P(School 1∩Pass) &= p^(^)(Student is from School 1) \cdot p^(^)(Student passes) = 0.28 \\ P(School 1∩Fail) &= p^(^)(Student is from School 1) \cdot p^(^)(Student fails) = 0.12 \\ P(School 2∩Pass) &= p^(^)(Student is from School 2) \cdot p^(^)(Student passes) = 0.42 \\ P(School 2∩Fail) &= p^(^)(Student is from School 2) \cdot p^(^)(Student fails) = 0.18 \end{aligned} $$ This gives the following table of probabilities: | | Pass | Fail | | --- | ---: | ---: | | School 1 | $0.28$ | $0.12$ | | School 2 | $0.42$ | $0.18$ | Let $E_{ij}$ denote the expected frequency in the $i$th row and $j$th column. To calculate the expected frequencies, we multiply each probability by $N=60$, the total number of sample elements. For example, $$ E_{11} = 60\cdot 0.28 = 16.8 $$ Adding these values to our original table, we get the following: | | Pass | Fail | | --- | ---: | ---: | | School 1 | $O_{11}=18$
$E_{11} =\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}16.8}$ | $O_{12}=6$
$E_{12} =\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}7.2}$ | | School 2 | $O_{18}=24$
$E_{21} =\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}25.2}$ | $O_{12}=12$
$E_{22} =\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}10.8}$ | Here, $O_{ij}$ is the *observed* frequency in the $i$th row and $j$th column. Now that we've seen a concrete example, let's generalize a little.

Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a sufficiently large population with sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}.$ Let's also assume that the following conditions are satisfied:

- $n \widehat{\,p} > 5$

- $n (1-\widehat{\,p}) > 5$

Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is given by

$$
\left(
\widehat{\,p} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}},\:

\widehat{\,p} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}
\right).
$$

The endpoints of our confidence interval are the **confidence limits** and are given by

$$
\widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}.
$$

Each part of the formula above has a name:

- $\!\widehat{\,p}$ is the sample proportion

- $p$ is the population proportion

- $n$ is the sample size

- $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $z$-score

- $E = z_{\alpha/2}\cdot  \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}$ is the margin of error

![](images/d0/d07c13f30dc4a0960b70f2705bb615f79c0c7ef3a6ed5d7a8eef2401db02d6c2.svg)

So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overset{^}{\,p}-[\text{margin of error}], & \,\overset{^}{\,p}+[\text{margin of error}]) \\ (\overset{^}{\,p}-[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}], & \,\overset{^}{\,p}+[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}]) \\ (\overset{^}{\,p}-{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}}, & \,\overset{^}{\,p}+{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}})\end{aligned}
$$

Since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably.

Finally, in the future, you may assume that if a population is "large," it is sufficiently larger than any sample drawn from it.

Earlier, we made use of the following results:

$$
\textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_1] = \beta_1,
\qquad
\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_1}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}
$$

Let's now derive these. First, we will show that

$$
S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})y_i.
$$

We can show this is true using some straightforward manipulations of the summation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})\overset{―}{y} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\overset{―}{x} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}n\overset{―}{x} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using our result for $S_{xy},$ we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{{\beta }_{1}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{{S}_{xx}}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
k_i = \dfrac{ x_i-\overline{x}}{S_{xx}}.
$$

The following properties can be shown using straightforward algebra:

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i=0$

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i x_i=1$

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i^2=\dfrac{1}{S_{xx}}$

Now, we compute the mean and variance of $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as follows:

- For the mean, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{{\beta }_{1}}] & =\text{E}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}\text{E}[{y}_{i}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\beta }_{0}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}+{\beta }_{1}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & ={\beta }_{0}\cdot 0+{\beta }_{1}\cdot 1 \\  & ={\beta }_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the properties of $k_i$ discussed previously.

- For the variance, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{{\beta }_{1}}] & =\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{y}_{i}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}^{2}\cdot {\sigma }^{2} \\  & ={\sigma }^{2}\cdot {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{{S}_{xx}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\widehat{\beta_1} \sim N\left(\beta_1, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\right).
$$

$$

$$

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i x_i=1$

$$

$$

$$

Consider a population where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Suppose we do *not* have an estimate for $p$, yet we want the smallest sample size $n$ required to ensure that the margin of error for a $95\%$ confidence interval is at most $0.03$. Is this even possible without an estimate for $p$?

As we saw previously, the minimum sample size is given by

$$
n \geq \dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 \, \widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{\varepsilon^2}
$$

We do not know $\widehat{\,p}$, and consequently, we do not know $\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})$ either. However, to find a lower bound for $n$, we can simply replace the expression $\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})$ with its maximum value for $\widehat{\,p}\in [0,1]$.

A plot of the function $\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})$ for different values of $\widehat{\,p}$ is given below.

![](images/d1/d1ea9a3d120e0cd3907308a00182d86c94f1b8e23c61ec146e6b49c2ace93ea8.png)

From the diagram, we see that the maximum value of $\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})$ occurs when

$$
\widehat{\,p} = \dfrac12
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})$ is

$$
\dfrac12\cdot \left(1-\dfrac12\right) = \dfrac14
$$

Substituting

$$
\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p}) = \dfrac14, \qquad z_{\alpha/2}=1.96, \qquad \varepsilon=0.03
$$

into our inequality for $n$, we finally arrive at

$$
n \mid \ge (z_{α/2}^{2}p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(ε^{2}); = ((1.96)^{2})/((0.03)^{2}) \cdot \frac{1}{4}; \approx 1067.11
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the sample size must be at least $n= 1068$.

Finally, note that when $\widehat{\,p}$ is unknown, we often require a significantly larger sample size to ensure the same margin of error compared to the case where $\widehat{\,p}$ is known.

Suppose a population is normally distributed with known mean $\mu$ and *unknown* variance $\sigma^2$. We can use empirical data to *estimate* the variance.

For example, let's assume our normal population has mean $\mu = 12$ and unknown variance. Suppose an independent random sample is drawn from the population, and it is found that approximately $68\%$ of the data in the sample have a value between $7$ and $17$.

According to the empirical rule, we have the following:

- Approximately $68\%$ of the data falls within $1$ standard deviation of the mean.
- Approximately $95\%$ of the data falls within $2$ standard deviations of the mean.
- Approximately $99.7\%$ of the data falls within $3$ standard deviations of the mean.

We can assume that $100\%$ of the data falls within $4$ (or more) standard deviations of the mean.

![](images/53/530392e9b21a099bfc6a4f4cbee2ac4adba729cfbcfa3127ded2ebbe60e85a45.png)

So, according to this rule, $68\%$ of the observations of a random normal variable $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ fall in the interval $(\mu-\sigma, \mu+\sigma)$. This range represents $2$ standard deviations. Therefore, we can write:

$$
\begin{aligned}
μ - σ^(^) &= 7 \\
μ + σ^(^) &= 17
\end{aligned}
$$

We have used $\widehat{\sigma}$ since the sample data will give an *estimate* of the population standard deviation $\sigma$. Since the observations used to formulate these equations came from sample data, we cannot assume that

$$
\widehat{\sigma} = \sigma
$$

However, if the sample is large, $\widehat{\sigma}$ should give a reasonable approximation to $\sigma$.

We wish to solve for $\widehat{\sigma}$. First, we subtract the first equation from the second, which gives

$$
2\widehat{\sigma} = 17-7 = 10
$$

Therefore,

$$
\widehat{\sigma} = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5
$$

Finally, the estimate of the population variance is given by

$$
\widehat{\sigma}^2 = 5^2 = 25
$$

Given a dataset of paired numerical observations $(x,y)$ and the corresponding linear regression model $\widehat{y} =f(x),$ the **residual** for a particular observation $(x, y)$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Residual} & =\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated} \\  & =y-f(x) \\  & =y-\overset{^}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

We subtract the *estimated* value predicted by the model from the actual *observed* value.

To illustrate this concept graphically, consider the following example.

The owner of an ice cream shop keeps track of the average daily temperature $x$ (measured in $^\circ \mathrm{F}$) and the resulting daily ice cream sales $y$ (in dollars). The scatter plot for several randomly selected days and the corresponding linear regression line are shown below. 

![](images/fc/fc149b8d911a7a9863df9cc25c635d6155accd676e83e335a65d9083596b779b.png)

Suppose the equation of the regression line is

$$
y= 2.5 x +165.
$$

Let's use our regression line to compute the residual of the point with coordinates $\color{red}(82, 360)$ (shown in red on our graph). 

First, notice that since the highlighted data point has coordinates ${\color{red}(82, 360)},$ our actual value is $y = {\color{red}360}.$

Next, we compute the predicted value using our linear regression model:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{y} & =2.5x+165 \\  & =2.5(82)+165 \\  & =370\end{aligned}
$$

 

![](images/38/3843c71b50251ae035378507ffb22cfade48dff8e1544d8e1317e4e6d611f7a1.png)

Finally, we compute the residual: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Residual} & =\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated} \\  & =y-\overset{^}{y} \\  & =360-370 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

     

The residual tells us that the linear model *overestimates* the true volume of ice cream sales by $\[math]10$ when the outside temperature is $82^\circ\,\textrm{F}.$

Suppose $X_1, X_2, \ldots X_n$ is a sequence of random variables representing a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a population with population mean $\mu$ and population variance $\sigma^2.$ Then the sample variance $S^2$ is given by

$$
S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2 = \dfrac{n}{n-1} \left[ \overline{X^2} - \left( \overline{X} \right)^2 \right] .
$$

Note that

- $\overline{X}$ is the sample mean,

- the sample variance $S^2$ is an unbiased estimator of the population variance $\sigma^2,$ and

- $\hat{\sigma}^2  = s^2$ denotes the unbiased estimate of $\sigma^2$ computed from the sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.$

First, we will compute the quantity

$$
\overline{x^2} - \left( \overline{x} \right)^2.
$$

We proceed as follows:

- The mean of the data is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{x} & =\frac{1}{5}(5+3+6+4+7) \\  & =\frac{25}{5} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

- The mean of the squared data is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{{x}^{2}} & =\frac{1}{5}({5}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{6}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{7}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{135}{5} \\  & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}-{(\overset{―}{x})}^{2} & =27-{5}^{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the sample variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\overset{^}{\sigma }}^{2} & ={s}^{2} \\  & =\frac{n}{n-1}[\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}-{(\overset{―}{x})}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{5}{5-1}\cdot 2 \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, an unbiased estimate of the population variance is $2.5.$

Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \right),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np > 5,$ and $n(1-p) > 5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n = 84,$ and

- the population proportion is $p = 0.42.$

Now, since

$$
np = 84(0.42) = 35.28 > 5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p) = 84(1-0.42) = 48.72 > 5,
$$

and $n=84$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.42,\frac{0.42(1-0.42)}{84}) \\  & ∼N(0.42,0.0029).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(\widehat{\,p} > 0.5).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.5) & =P(Z>\frac{0.5-0.42}{\sqrt{0.0029}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.49) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.49) \\  & =1-Φ(1.49).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.49) & =0.9319.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.5) & =1-Φ(1.49) \\  & =1-0.9319 \\  & =0.0681.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),

where

- $np>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and

- $n(1-p)>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =16,\, \\ 5%\cdot N & =0.05\cdot 100 \\  & =5 \\  & <16.\,\times \end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =32 \\  & \le 5%\cdot N \\  & =0.05\cdot 1\,000 \\  & =50\,✓ \\ np & =32(0.1) \\  & =3.2 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since $np≯5,$ we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =32 \\  & \le 5%\cdot N \\  & =0.05\cdot 1\,000 \\  & =50\,✓ \\ np & =32(0.75) \\  & =24 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =32(1-0.75) \\  & =8 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

$$

$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept ${\beta }_{0}$ of our model can be written as

$$
\underbrace{{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}}_{\,\,\text{point}\,\text{estimate}}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{18,0.025}=2.101.
$$

$$

$$

Let's now derive these. First, we will show that

$$
S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})y_i.
$$

We can show this is true using some straightforward manipulations of the summation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})\overset{―}{y} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\overset{―}{x} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}n\overset{―}{x} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we define $k_i$ as

$$
k_i = \dfrac{ x_i-\overline{x}}{S_{xx}}.
$$

The following properties can be shown using straightforward algebra:

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i=0$

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i x_i=1$

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i^2=\dfrac{1}{S_{xx}}$

Now, recall that

$$
\widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} - \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{{\beta }_{0}} & =\overset{―}{y}-{\beta }_{1}\overset{―}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}-\frac{{S}_{xy}}{{S}_{xx}}\overset{―}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}-\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}}{{S}_{xx}}\overset{―}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}\overset{―}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{{\beta }_{0}}] & =\frac{1}{n}\text{E}[{\sum }_{i}{y}_{i}]-\overset{―}{x}\text{E}[{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}\text{E}[{y}_{i}]-\overset{―}{x}{\sum }_{i}\text{E}[{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}[{\beta }_{0}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}+{\beta }_{1}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{x}_{i}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}[{\beta }_{0}{\cancel{{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}}}^{0}+{\beta }_{1}{\cancel{{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{x}_{i}}}^{1}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1} \\  & =\frac{{\beta }_{0}}{n}{\sum }_{i}1+\frac{{\beta }_{1}}{n}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1} \\  & =\frac{{\beta }_{0}}{n}\cdot n+\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1}-\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1} \\  & ={\beta }_{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the variance, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{{\beta }_{0}}] & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i}{y}_{i}]+{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}{\sum }_{i}\text{Var}[{y}_{i}]+{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{y}_{i}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}n{\sigma }^{2}+{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}^{2}{\sigma }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}n{\sigma }^{2}+{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}{\sigma }^{2}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sigma }^{2}+{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}{\sigma }^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{S}_{xx}} \\  & ={\sigma }^{2}(\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}}).\end{aligned}
$$

So finally, we have

$$
\widehat{\beta_0} \sim N\left(\beta_0,\sigma^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right).
$$

Given a population of $N$ individuals in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p} \sim N\left(p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \right)
$$

where

- $n$ is the sample size,
- $np > 5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and
- $n(1-p) > 5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

The factor

$$
\dfrac{N-n}{N-1}
$$

is the finite population correction factor for the variance. This is used in cases of finite samples where

- $n\gt 5\%\cdot N$ (i.e., the sample comprises more than $5\%$ of the population), and
- The sample is conducted without replacement.

If a sample is conducted from a finite population *with replacement*, then the sample data are independent, and a finite population correction factor is not required.

In our case, we have

$$
n = 30, \qquad p = 0.25, \qquad N = 100
$$

Now, since

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle n & \displaystyle  > 5 \mathrm{\% } \cdot  100 = 5 \\ \displaystyle n p & \displaystyle  = 30 ( 0.25 ) = 7.5 > 5 \\ \displaystyle n ( 1 - p ) & \displaystyle  = 30 ( 0.75 ) = 22.5 > 5\end{array}}
$$

we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
p^(^) \mid ∼N(p, (p(1 - p))/(n) \cdot \frac{N - n}{N - 1}); ∼N(0.25, (0.25(1 - 0.25))/(30) \cdot \frac{70}{99}); ∼N(0.25, \frac{7}{1584})
$$

$$

Recall that the $k$th sample moment $M_k$ of a sample $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is given by

$$
M_k = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^k
$$

In particular, the first and second sample moments are given by

$$
M_1 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \,, \qquad M_2 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2
$$

To find the method of moments estimator for a parameter, we calculate a sample moment and the corresponding theoretical moment and equate them.

We are given the sum of the squared values in the sample. So, we can calculate the second sample moment:

$$
m_2 = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 = \dfrac{140}{5}=28
$$

We are given that the variables follow a uniform distribution $U(a,b)$. Therefore,

$$
\textrm{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}
$$

We also have

$$
\textrm{Var}[X_i] = \textrm{E}[X^2_i] - \left(\textrm{E}[X_i]\right)^2
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the second theoretical moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X_{i}^{2}] &= Var[X_{i}] + (E[X_{i}])^{2} \\
&= (((θ + 6) - θ)^{2})/(12) + ((θ + (θ + 6))/(2))^{2} \\
&= \frac{36}{12} + (θ + 3)^{2} \\
&= 3 + θ^{2} + 6θ + 9 \\
&= θ^{2} + 6θ + 12
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the sample and theoretical second moments and using the estimator $\widehat\theta_{MM}$ in place of $\theta$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
θ^(^)_{MM}^{2} + 6θ^(^)_{MM} + 12 &= 28
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for $\widehat\theta_{MM}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
θ^(^)_{MM}^{2} + 6θ^(^)_{MM} + 12 &= 28 \\
θ^(^)_{MM}^{2} + 6θ^(^)_{MM} - 16 &= 0 \\
(θ^(^)_{MM} + 8)(θ^(^)_{MM} - 2) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions

$$
\widehat{\theta}_{MM}= -8, \qquad \widehat{\theta}_{MM}= 2
$$

However, we discard the negative solution since we are given that $\theta > 0$. Therefore, our method of moments estimate for $\theta$ is

$$
\widehat{\theta}_{MM}= \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2}
$$

Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=8%=0.08,$ and $n=100.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =8%=0.08, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.08(1-0.08)}{100} \\  & ≈0.0007\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=15%=0.15,$ and $n=18.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =15%=0.15, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.15(1-0.15)}{18} \\  & ≈0.007\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…{X}_{n}$ is a sequence of random variables representing a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2}.$ Then, the sample variance ${S}^{2}$ is given by

$$
{S}^{2}=\frac{1}{n-1}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})}^{2}=\frac{n}{n-1}[\overset{―}{{X}^{2}}-{(\overset{―}{X})}^{2}].
$$

Note that:

- $\overset{―}{X}$ is the sample mean,

- the sample variance ${S}^{2}$ is an unbiased estimator of the population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ and

- ${\overset{^}{\sigma }}^{2}={s}^{2}$ denotes an unbiased estimate of ${\sigma }^{2}$ that's computed from the sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}.$

We're given that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{51}{({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}=24.5$ and $n=51.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\overset{^}{\sigma }}^{2} & ={s}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{51-1}\cdot 24.5 \\  & =\frac{1}{50}\cdot 24.5 \\  & =0.49.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, an unbiased estimate of the population variance is ${\overset{^}{\sigma }}^{2}=0.49.$ We take the square root to compute an unbiased estimate of the standard deviation. This gives

$$
\overset{^}{\sigma }=\sqrt{0.49}=0.7.
$$

Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=60%=0.6,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =60%=0.6, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.6(1-0.6)}{20} \\  & =0.012.\end{aligned}
$$

Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=99,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.45.$

Now, since

$$
np=99(0.45)=44.55>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=99(1-0.45)=54.45>5,
$$

and $n=99$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.45,\frac{0.45(1-0.45)}{99}) \\  & ∼N(0.45,0.0025).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(\overset{^}{\,p}<0.5).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}<0.5) & =P(Z<\frac{0.5-0.45}{\sqrt{0.0025}}) \\  & =P(Z<1.00) \\  & =Φ(1.00).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.00) & =0.8413.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}<0.5) & =Φ(0.8413) \\  & =0.8413.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where 

- $n\le 5%\cdot N$ (the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5%$ of the population size),

- $np>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and

- $n(1-p)>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =52, \\ 5%\cdot N & =0.05\cdot 120 \\  & =6 \\  & <52.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size is more than $5%$ of the population size, we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =4 \\  & \le 5%\cdot N \\  & =0.05\cdot 200 \\  & =10\,✓ \\ np & =4(0.7) \\  & =2.8 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since $np≯5,$ we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation III, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =20 \\  & \le 5%\cdot N \\  & =0.05\cdot 500 \\  & =25\,✓ \\ np & =20(0.70) \\  & =14 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =20(1-0.70) \\  & =6 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=96,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.72.$

Now, since

$$
np=96(0.72)=69.12>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=96(1-0.72)=26.88>5,
$$

and $n=96$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.72,\frac{0.72(1-0.72)}{96}) \\  & ∼N(0.72,0.0021).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.8).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.8) & =P(\frac{0.7-0.72}{\sqrt{0.0021}}<Z\le \frac{0.8-0.72}{\sqrt{0.0021}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.44<Z\le 1.75) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.75)-P(Z\le -0.44) \\  & =Φ(1.75)-Φ(-0.44)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.75) & =0.9599 \\ Φ(-0.44) & =0.3300.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.8) & =Φ(1.75)-Φ(-0.44) \\  & =0.9599-0.3300 \\  & =0.6299.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's interpret the data:

- the population consists of all U.S. internet users,

- some internet subscribers are satisfied with their current internet provider, and some aren't,

- the size of the random sample is $n=800,$ and

- the proportion of Internet subscribers from the sample who are satisfied with their current internet provider is found as follows:

$$
\overset{^}{p\,}=\frac{560}{800}=0.7
$$

Now, we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=800\cdot 0.7=560>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=800\cdot (1-0.7)=240>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation: 

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

 

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.005}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.005})=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$

![](images/f5/f5e154855d4a4f18fb81d522873fb29c11fd7c9543ffebdeac0f15672c7e72b2.png)

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.005}=2.576:$  

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0,7\pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.7(1-0.7)}{800}} \\  & 0.7\pm 0.042\end{aligned}
$$

Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=224,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=\frac{56\,000}{100\,000}=0.56.$

Now, since

$$
np=224(0.56)=125.44>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=224(1-0.56)=98.56>5,
$$

and the $n=224$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.56,\frac{0.56(1-0.56)}{224}) \\  & ∼N(0.56,0.0011).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If between $112$ and $140$ of subscribers in the sample have a digital subscription, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{112}{224}\le \overset{^}{\,p} & \le \frac{140}{224} \\ 0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p} & \le 0.625.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.625).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.625) & =P(\frac{0.5-0.56}{\sqrt{0.0011}}\le Z\le \frac{0.625-0.56}{\sqrt{0.0011}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.81\le Z\le 1.96) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.96)-P(Z\le -1.81) \\  & =Φ(1.96)-Φ(-1.81)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.96)=0.9750,\,Φ(-1.81)=0.0351.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.625) & =Φ(1.96)-Φ(-1.81) \\  & =0.9750-0.0351 \\  & =0.9399.\end{aligned}
$$

Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where 

- $n\le 5%\cdot N$ (the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5%$ of the population size),

- $np>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and

- $n(1-p)>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

We're given that the population is significantly larger than the sample size in each case. Therefore, we may assume that the first condition is satisfied in each case.

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =50(0.6) \\  & =30 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =50(1-0.6) \\  & =20 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =60(0.8) \\  & =48 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =60(1-0.8) \\  & =12 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation III, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =40(0.9) \\  & =36 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =40(1-0.9) \\  & =4 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),

- $n(1-p)>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

$$

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=5+0.4x.
$$

$$
\underbrace{{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}}_{\,\,\text{point}\,\text{estimate}}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.

$$

$$

We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=-26.6+0.5x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}$ is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{{S}_{xx}}}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=-26.6+0.5x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}=0.5.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(T>2.92)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.05}=2.92.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(67-71.5)^{2}+(70-71.5)^{2}+(73-71.5)^{2}+(76-71.5)^{2} \\  & =20.25+2.25+2.25+20.25 \\  & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=2.92\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.338}{45}}≈0.3
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=0.5\pm 0.3
$$

Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=38%=0.38,$ and $n=30.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =38%=0.38, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.38(1-0.38)}{30} \\  & ≈0.008\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
